summary: This note surveys the geography of the United States, covering its climate zones, the Great Lakes and river systems, the capital and overseas territories, and regional weather hazards. It describes arid western basins, the hot Southwest and monsoon effects, and the tornado, hurricane, flood, drought and wildfire risks in different regions. It closes with the interior plains and how their climate shapes vegetation.
one_line: Overview of US geography covering climate zones, Great Lakes and river systems, overseas territories, regional weather hazards, and interior plains.
key_facts: The United States contains examples of nearly every global climate due to its large size and wide range of geographic features.
The climate is subtropical in the Southern United States and tropical in Hawaii and southern Florida.
The climate is polar in Alaska and Mediterranean in coastal California, while the Great Basin is arid.
The five Great Lakes are located in the north-central portion of the country, and only Lake Michigan lies entirely within the United States.
Washington, District of Columbia, is a federal district located on land donated by the state of Maryland.
Virginia had also donated land for the capital, but that land was returned in 1849.
The Great Basin and Columbia Plateau are arid or semiarid regions in the rain shadow of the Cascades and Sierra Nevada.
Precipitation in the Great Basin and Columbia Plateau averages less than 15 inches (38 cm).
The Southwest is a hot desert where temperatures exceed 100 °F (37.8 °C) for several weeks at a time in summer.
The monsoon from the Gulf of California affects the Southwest and Great Basin from July to September, bringing localized but often severe thunderstorms.
In central portions of the U.S., tornadoes are more common than anywhere else on Earth, most often in spring and summer.
The Southwest has the worst droughts; one is thought to have lasted over 500 years and to have hurt Ancestral Pueblo peoples.
The Appalachian region and the Midwest experience the worst floods, though virtually no area in the U.S. is immune to flooding.
The Ohio and Tennessee Valleys and the Midwest consist largely of rolling hills and productive farmland, stretching south to the Gulf Coast.
From the United States side, the great Mississippi system discharges southward to the Gulf of Mexico.
